To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
integration of high-risk HPV genomes in cervical cancer is a consequence rather the cause of chromosal instability.

the frequency of integration of oncogenic human papillomaviruses (HR-HPVs) into host cell genomes is type-dependent and that the time required for high-grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasias (CINs) induced by HR-HPVs to progress to invasive cervical cancers is also type-dependent.

the integration frequency of HPV genomes is type-dependent, that HPV types 16, 18 and 45 are found more frequently in the integrated state in carcinomas compared with types 31 and33 and that precancers associated with HPV types 18 and 16 progress to invasive cancers in less time than precancers induced by the other types.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and evaluation of molecular diagnostic tests and the analysis of the role of human papilloma virus (HPV) in the development of cervical cancer.
the development of new molecular tools for the detection of HPV DNA in the cervical samples and for the analysis of the integration status of HPV genomes in cervical samples.
the integration status of HPV genomes in cervical cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the integration of HPV DNA into host chromosomes is not a sufficient condition to promote the progression of cervical precancers to invasive cancers.
the integration status of HPV genomes in cervical cancers is not a reliable predictor of the HPV type associated with the tumor.
the integration of HR-HPVs in cervical lesions is not an absolute requirement to achieve neoplasia but that the frequency of integration is dependent on the type of HPV.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the integration of HR-HPVs into the host cell genome does not represent the cause but rather the consequence of the carcinogenic process.
the integration of HR-HPVs is a consequence rather then the cause of chromosomally instability in cervical cancers.
HPV16, 45 and 18 have a higher tendency to integrate into the host genome than HPV31 and 33 and that this integration is associated with a higher risk of progressing to invasive cancer.
The main takeaway from our work is that

HPV integration is not a prerequisite to cancer development, and that the integration status of HPV DNA in cervical cancers may be a consequence rather than a cause of the neoplastic transformation process.
integration of HR-HPVs in advanced lesions is a consequence and not a cause of chromosomal aberrations in cervical cancer.
the frequency of integration of oncogenic human papillomaviruses in cervical lesions depends on the type of the virus.
